source_text: CAPUT DECIMUMSEXTUM, De voluntate Dei. Haec Dei imago est: voluntas est illius vita, qua Deus in bonum cognitum fertur. Voluntatem Deo recte tribui tum essentiae et intellectus Dei perfectio, tum Scriptura, hominumque consensus abunde confirmant — Jonae I.14; Dan. IV.17; Rom. IX.18; Jac. I.18; Psal. CXV.3; Matth. XX.15; Ephes. I.11. Cum autem definitur orexis noera, appetitus rationalis, Deo proprie hoc sensu non tribui recte notat CL. P. Molinaeus, quia nec ratio proprie Deo competit.
english: CHAPTER SIXTEEN. On the will of God.

This is God's image: will is that life of His by which God is borne toward a known good. That will is rightly attributed to God, both the perfection of God's essence and intellect, and Scripture, and the consent of men abundantly confirm — Jonah 1:14; Daniel 4:17; Romans 9:18; James 1:18; Psalm 115:3; Matthew 20:15; Ephesians 1:11.
But when it is defined as rational appetite, the learned Molina rightly notes that it is not properly attributed to God in this sense, because reason also does not properly belong to God.

source_text: III. Objectum est bonum ab intellectu cognitum. Voluntas enim fertur in bonum cognitum. Deum vero velle ita probamus a Scripturae testimoniis, ab essentiae perfectione, ab intellectu, a spirituali vita, ab operationibus internis et externis, a consensu ecclesiae et philosophorum. Voluntas Dei est summa illius perfectio, qua essentia ipsius excellenter fertur in bonum a se cognitum.
english: III. The object is the good known by the intellect. For will is borne toward a known good. That God truly wills we prove from the testimonies of Scripture, from perfection of essence, from intellect, from spiritual life, from inward and outward operations, from the consent of the church and of the philosophers.
The will of God is His highest perfection, by which His essence is excellently borne toward the good known by Himself.

source_text: VII. PRIMO enim Dei voluntas est naturalis aut libera. VIII. Naturalis est qua Deus secundum necessitatem naturae suae vult. X. SECUNDO, Dei voluntas libera est. XI. Voluntas signi est qua Deus significat creaturis quid velit ab ipsis fieri. XII. Voluntas beneplaciti est qua Deus apud se decretum constituit de rebus faciendis aut permittendis.
english: VII. FIRST, God's will is natural or free. VIII. Natural is that by which God wills according to the necessity of His nature. X. SECOND, God's will is free. XI. The will of sign is that by which God signifies to creatures what He wills to be done by them. XII. The will of good pleasure is that by which God establishes with Himself a decree concerning things to be done or permitted.

source_text: XVI. TERTIO, voluntas Dei est absoluta aut conditionata. XVII. Absoluta est qua Deus aliquid vult sine conditione. XVIII. Conditionata est qua Deus aliquid vult sub conditione. XIX. QUARTO, voluntas Dei est antecedens aut consequens. Voluntas antecedens est qua Deus vult aliquid priusquam considerentur circumstantiae particulares; consequens qua, positis circumstantiis, vult. Haec dici potest voluntas judiciaria — sicut magistratus voluntate antecedente vult omnes cives vivos esse, consequente aliquos mori propter scelera; sic Deus voluntate antecedente vult omnes homines salvos fieri, I Tim. II.4, voluntate consequente credentibus justitiam confert, impoenitentibus mortem aeternam infligit.
english: XVI. THIRD, God's will is absolute or conditioned. XVII. Absolute is that by which God wills something without condition. XVIII. Conditioned is that by which God wills something under a condition. XIX. FOURTH, God's will is antecedent or consequent.

Antecedent will is that by which God wills something before particular circumstances are considered; consequent that by which, circumstances being posited, He wills. This can be called judicial will — as a magistrate by antecedent will wants all citizens alive, by consequent will some to die for crimes; so God by antecedent will wants all men to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), by consequent will confers righteousness on believers and inflicts eternal death on the impenitent.

source_text: XXII. QUINTO, voluntas Dei est approbans, aut efficiens, aut permittens. Alii distinguunt eodem sensu in voluntatem approbationis et decreti. XXIII. Approbans est qua Deus aliquid amat tanquam bonum possibile a natura sua haud dissentaneum, quod tamen non efficiat. XXIV. Efficiens est qua Deus vult aliquid producere, et aliquid in aliquo aut per aliquid operari. XXV. Permittens est qua aliquid fieri vult, quamvis oderit, propter bonum conjunctum, non impedire — sic Deus lapsum primorum parentum permittere voluit, Rom. IX.17; Act. IV.28.
english: XXII. FIFTH, God's will is approving, or efficient, or permitting. Others distinguish in the same sense into the will of approbation and of decree. XXIII. Approving is that by which God loves something as a possible good not dissonant from His nature, which yet He does not effect. XXIV. Efficient is that by which God wills to produce something, and to work something in or through something. XXV. Permitting is that by which He wills something to happen which, though He hates it, He does not impede because of a joined good — so God willed to permit the fall of the first parents, Romans 9:17; Acts 4:28.

source_text: XXVI. SEXTO, voluntas Dei est arcana aut revelata. XXVII. Arcana est quae creaturae intelligenti, quamdiu Deo visum, abscondita est — beneplacitum Ephes. I; non est perscrutanda, Deut. XXIX.29. XXVIII. Revelata est quae signo Dei aut eventu rei patefacta est — voluntas signi. XXIX-XXXI. Estque praecisa aut modificata. XXXII-XXXIV. Estque ampla aut limitata. XXXV-XXXVIII. Estque exploratoria, promissoria, aut comminatoria — ut Abrahami sacrificium Gen. XXII; promissiones et comminationes sub tacita conditione.
english: XXVI. SIXTH, God's will is arcane or revealed. XXVII. Arcane is that which is hidden from the intelligent creature as long as it seems good to God — the good pleasure of Ephesians 1; it is not to be searched out, Deuteronomy 29:29. XXVIII. Revealed is that which is made plain by God's sign or by the event of the thing — the will of sign.

XXIX–XXXI. And it is precise or modified. XXXII–XXXIV. And it is ample or limited. XXXV–XXXVIII. And it is exploratory, promissory, or minatory — as Abraham's sacrifice in Genesis 22; promises and threats under a tacit condition.

source_text: XXXIX. SEPTIMO, voluntas Dei est ordinaria aut extraordinaria. XL. Ordinaria est qua Deus ordinem semel a se constitutum in operibus naturae et donis gratiae constanter servat. XLI. Extraordinaria est qua Deus praeter et supra hunc ordinem pro sua sapientia et arbitrio agit — hinc miracula. XLII. OCTAVO, voluntas Dei est per se aut propter aliud et per accidens. XLIII. Voluntas Dei per se est qua Deus vult quae simpliciter bona sunt. XLIV. Voluntas Dei propter aliud est qua vult quae respectu quodam mala sunt, at ordinabilia in bonum — licet Deo velle ut evenerit peccatum ipso permittente propter bonum conjunctum. Ex his de Dei voluntate probe constitutis nemini obscurum esse potest, Deo nihil esse melius, nihil benignius, nihil sanctius, nihil justius — fundamentum totius religionis et consolationis nostrae. CAPUT DECIMUMSEPTIMUM, De potentia Dei exsequente, sequitur.
english: XXXIX. SEVENTH, God's will is ordinary or extraordinary. XL. Ordinary is that by which God constantly keeps the order once established by Himself in the works of nature and the gifts of grace. XLI. Extraordinary is that by which God acts beside and above this order according to His wisdom and choice — hence miracles.

XLII. EIGHTH, God's will is through itself or for another and by accident. XLIII. God's will through itself is that by which God wills things simply good. XLIV. God's will for another is that by which He wills things which in a certain respect are evil, yet ordainable unto good — it is lawful for God to will that sin should have happened with Him permitting, because of a joined good.

From these things rightly established concerning God's will it can be obscure to none that nothing is better than God, nothing kinder, nothing holier, nothing more just — the foundation of all our religion and consolation. CHAPTER SEVENTEEN, On God's executive power, follows.
